claims.label: The wave is real
claims.summary: Schrödinger hoped the wave was a real physical process: for one electron ψψ* gives a continuous charge density, stationary states are proper vibrations, and discrete frequencies arise as in a vibrating string, without jumps.
voice: My hope has been that the wave is not a bookkeeping device. For one electron, ψψ* gives a density of charge, continuous in space and time, and the stationary states are simply proper vibrations. The discrete frequencies come out of a boundary-value problem, as the tones of a string do. We need not assume jumps to obtain them.
Emitted light has the frequency of a beat between two proper vibrations. That is a picture one can hold in the mind.
claims.reasoning: Quantisation emerges naturally as an eigenvalue problem; emission frequencies appear as beat frequencies between vibrations.
evidence: The hydrogen spectrum from an eigenvalue problem.
objections: Configuration space: for several particles the wave lives in many dimensions.
Bohr, Heisenberg: discrete individual processes cannot come from continuous waves alone.
claims.later: The charge-density reading did not survive, but the reality of the wave is defended today in pilot-wave and many-worlds theories.

claims.label: Repelled by matrix methods
claims.summary: Schrödinger wrote that he had been discouraged, not to say repelled, by the transcendental algebra of matrix mechanics and its lack of visualisability.
voice: I knew Heisenberg's theory and admired its results. But I was discouraged — repelled, even — by its methods of transcendental algebra and its renunciation of any picture. I do not think physics should give up visualisability until it has been shown to be impossible, not merely inconvenient.
claims.reasoning: A picture guides discovery; abandoning it should be a last resort.

claims.label: No quantum jumping
claims.summary: Schrödinger found the idea of discontinuous quantum jumps unacceptable; Heisenberg recalled him saying in Copenhagen in 1926 that if the jumping were to stay he would regret having worked on quantum theory.
voice: The idea of quantum jumps makes no sense to me — an electron sitting in an orbit, then leaping without anything happening in between. If discontinuous jumping is really to remain in the theory, I confess I shall regret having taken any part in it.
Bohr pressed me on this for days in Copenhagen last year. I was ill by the end of it, and I was not persuaded.
claims.reasoning: A continuous wave process should underlie emission; jumps are an unexplained discontinuity.
claims.exchangeNote: Copenhagen, October 1926, as recalled by Heisenberg.

claims.label: Configuration space: unsolved
claims.summary: In his Solvay report Schrödinger acknowledged that for many particles ψ is a function in configuration space, whose physical meaning is not yet clear, and proposed obtaining a charge density in ordinary space by integration.
voice: I do not hide the difficulty. For many electrons the wave lives in a space of many dimensions, and its meaning there is not yet clear to me. I have proposed to read it as a charge distribution in ordinary space, obtained by integrating over the other coordinates. It is not a finished answer.
claims.reasoning: Honest acknowledgement that the many-body case resists a simple ontology.

claims.label: Wave groups — partly
claims.summary: Schrödinger showed that for the harmonic oscillator a wave group holds together and moves like a classical particle; Lorentz pointed out that for the hydrogen atom such groups disperse, and Schrödinger acknowledged the difficulty.
voice: For the oscillator I could construct a wave group that holds together and swings like a classical particle. Lorentz rightly wrote to me that for the hydrogen atom such groups spread out. I have not yet found a way around it.
claims.reasoning: Partial success for the oscillator; failure in general.

claims.label: Probability not the last word
claims.summary: Schrödinger was not persuaded that Born's probabilities were final; by inference from his 1926–27 writings, he hoped they would follow from a continuous wave process not yet understood.
voice: I am not persuaded that probability is the last word. It may be that the statistical rules follow from a continuous wave process we do not yet fully understand. I would rather keep looking than declare the search closed.
claims.reasoning: If the wave is real, the statistics should be derivable from its dynamics.
